title: 1st Grade Place Value and Number Charts Worksheets (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: 1st Grade Place Value & Number Charts Worksheets
meta_desc: Teach 1st grade place value with tens, ones and a hundred chart. Beat the teen-number trap, play chart games, take a free quiz and grab worksheets.
excerpt: A hundred chart is the single most useful thing you can pin on the wall in Grade 1. Here is how place value, tens and ones, and the number chart fit together — plus a free quiz and printable practice.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Grade 1 child to point to 34 on a hundred chart and you learn a lot in three seconds. The child who counts every square from 1 has not met place value yet. The one who slides straight down to the fourth row and along to the fourth box already senses that 34 means ‘three full rows and four more’ — three tens and four ones. That is the whole idea of 1st grade place value, and a number chart is the cheapest, fastest way to build it.

This is the piece parents most often skip. They drill 1 + 1 and 2 + 3, then wonder why their child freezes at 27 or writes 15 as ‘51’. Addition is arithmetic; place value is how our whole number system is built. Get it wrong at six and every later topic — carrying, borrowing, larger numbers — wobbles. Get it right and the rest has a foundation to stand on.

What place value covers in Grade 1

Grade 1 keeps it deliberately small: numbers to about 99, split into tens and ones. A child needs to see that 46 is not the digits 4 and 6 sitting side by side — it is 4 tens and 6 ones, which is 40 and 6. The best way in is bundling. Give your child 46 matchsticks or straws and let them make bundles of ten with a rubber band. Four bundles and six loose sticks. Count the bundles by tens (10, 20, 30, 40) then the loose ones (41…46). Now the ‘4’ in 46 is not a four; it is four tens. That physical bundling does more than any worksheet in the first week.

  • Tens and ones — the two ‘jobs’ a digit can have, depending on where it sits.
  • Reading and writing numbers to 99 without swapping the digits.
  • Expanded form — writing 46 as 40 + 6.
  • Comparing numbers using the tens digit first (63 beats 59 because 6 tens beats 5 tens).

The teen-number trap

Here is the part that catches almost every six-year-old, and it is worth naming. The teen numbers — 11 to 19 — are the odd ones out in English. We say ‘twenty-three’ and hear the tens first, then the ones, in order. But we say ‘fourteen’ and ‘sixteen’, which puts the ones sound first, so children write 41 for fourteen and 61 for sixteen. It is not carelessness; the language is genuinely misleading.

Slow right down on the teens. Show 14 on the ten-frame as one full frame (ten) plus four extra dots, and on the hundred chart as the fourth box of the second row. Say it out loud as ‘ten and four’ before ‘fourteen’. In my experience teaching this age, a fortnight spent only on 11–19 saves months of place-value confusion later.

Using a hundred chart

A number chart — the 1-to-100 grid, ten columns wide — is the tool I would pin on the wall before buying anything else. Its power is that place value is baked into its shape. Move one square right and you add one. Move one square down and you add a whole ten. Once a child feels that, mental jumps like 34 + 10 = 44 or 58 − 10 = 48 become a single finger-slide down or up, no counting required.

Three hundred-chart games worth playing

  • Guess my number. You think of a number; the child asks ‘is it bigger than 50?’, ‘is it in the row starting with 30?’ and narrows it down. This drills the tens-first way of comparing.
  • Ten more, ten less. Call a number; the child slides one row down for ten more, one row up for ten less. Pure place-value muscle memory.
  • Cover and recall. Hide five squares with paper bits and ask what is underneath. The child reconstructs them from the pattern of rows and columns, not by counting from one.

Some charts run 0–99 instead of 1–100 so every row shares the same tens digit. Both are fine — pick one and stick with it so the child builds one clear mental picture rather than two half-formed ones.

Expanded form without the jargon

Expanded form sounds technical but it is just saying a number the long way: 72 is 70 + 2. Do not lead with the term. Start with the straw bundles — ‘seven bundles and two loose, so seventy and two’ — and only later attach the label. A child who can flip between 72, ‘7 tens and 2 ones’, and ‘70 + 2’ genuinely understands the number. That flexibility, not the vocabulary, is the goal.

How the tools line up

ToolBest forExample
Straw bundlesFirst meeting tens and ones46 = 4 bundles + 6

What a good worksheet should ask

Once the hands-on work has landed, written practice locks it in. A worksheet that only asks a child to circle the tens digit is too thin. Look for a mix: filling gaps in a hundred chart, matching 53 to ‘5 tens 3 ones’, writing numbers in expanded form, and a few ‘ten more, ten less’ rows. One honest caveat — do not rush a child onto paper. A week of bundling and chart games first makes the worksheets feel easy instead of baffling.

Try the quiz, then the worksheets

Below is a free, self-scoring quiz covering exactly this — tens and ones, teen numbers, the hundred chart and expanded form. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: 1st Grade Place Value Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on tens and ones, teen numbers, the hundred chart and expanded form. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 1 place value and number charts to 99

questions.q: In the number 47, what does the 4 stand for?
questions.explanation: The digit on the left is the tens. In 47 the 4 means 4 tens, which is 40.

questions.q: How do you write ‘fourteen’ as a number?
questions.explanation: Fourteen is ten and four, so it is 14. The teen numbers can trick you into writing the ones first.

questions.q: On a hundred chart, moving one square straight down adds how much?
questions.explanation: Each row is ten wide, so one square down is a whole ten more.

questions.q: Which number is the same as 6 tens and 3 ones?

questions.explanation: Adding ten means one slide down the hundred chart: 34 becomes 44.
Compare the tens first. 6 tens beats 5 tens, so 63 is bigger even though 9 is more than 3.
72 is 7 tens and 2 ones, so the long way is 70 + 2.
Taking ten away is one slide up the hundred chart: 58 becomes 48.

faq.q: What place value should a Grade 1 child know by the end of the year?
faq.a: Numbers to about 99 as tens and ones: reading and writing them without swapping digits, showing a number on a hundred chart or ten-frame, comparing two numbers, and writing simple expanded form like 46 = 40 + 6.

faq.q: Why does my child write 15 as 51?
faq.a: Almost always the teen-number trap. English says ‘fif-teen’ with the ones sound first, so children write the ones first. Slow down on 11–19, say each one as ‘ten and five’, and show it on a ten-frame.

faq.q: Do I need to buy a hundred chart?
faq.a: No. Print a plain 1–100 grid or draw a ten-by-ten square on paper. What matters is using it daily — moving right for one more and down for ten more — not how pretty it looks.

faq.q: How is a number chart different from just counting?
faq.a: Counting treats numbers as a flat list. A hundred chart shows their structure: every row is a ten, every column shares a ones digit. That is what turns 34 + 10 into a single finger-slide instead of ten separate counts.
